lessons.title: Lesson 1: Free and low-cost ways to get online
lessons.text:
Lesson 1 of 6 · about 5 minutes
Goal: Name two places near you where you can use the internet for free, and one program that can lower your phone or internet bill.
This lesson builds toward: Where you live, you will name free places to get online and one program that can lower your phone or internet bill, naming at least two places with their hours.
You do not need to own a computer to use technology. Public libraries have free computers and free Wi-Fi, and many also lend laptops or hotspots. Community centers, job centers and some churches have computers you can use too.
Lifeline is a federal program that lowers the monthly cost of phone or internet service for people with low income or who take part in programs like SNAP or Medicaid. You apply online, then pick a phone or internet company that takes part.
Library staff can help you get started. Asking for help is normal; helping people with computers is part of their job.
Step by step:
- Look up your nearest public library and its hours.
- Ask if it lends laptops or hotspots, and if it offers free computer classes.
- If money is tight, read about Lifeline on the official site and see if you qualify.
- Write down the place and time you will go online this week.
Words to know:
- Wi-Fi: a way to connect to the internet without a cable.
- Hotspot: a small device (or a phone setting) that shares an internet connection with other devices.
- Lifeline: a federal program that gives a monthly discount on phone or internet service to people who qualify.
Official sources:
- Lifeline Support (USAC, the official Lifeline site)
Try it now: Write down two places near you where you can use the internet for free, with their hours. If your phone or internet bill is hard to pay, open lifelinesupport.org and read who qualifies.
You can now name free places to get online and know where to learn about Lifeline.

check.q: What is a hotspot that some libraries lend?
options: A small device that lets you get on the internet
check.why: A hotspot is a small device that gives you internet so you can get online away from the library.

check.q: Your internet bill is hard to pay and you get SNAP. What do you do?
options: Read about Lifeline on the official site to see if you qualify
Ask a stranger online to pay it
Wait for the company to call you
check.why: Lifeline lowers the monthly cost for people with low income or in programs like SNAP.

lessons.title: Lesson 2: What AI is, in everyday words
lessons.text:
Lesson 2 of 6 · about 4 minutes
Goal: Explain what an AI assistant is and name three ways it could help your family.
This lesson builds toward: Given a list of everyday tasks, you will identify which ones an AI assistant can help with and who decides what to do with its answer, getting at least 4 of 5 right.
AI stands for artificial intelligence. An AI assistant is a program you can write to, or talk to, in your own words. It writes back an answer in seconds. Free ones include ChatGPT, Microsoft Copilot and Google Gemini.
It can explain a hard letter, write a short message, plan meals on a budget, help a child understand homework, or translate between languages.
It is a helper, not a boss. It does not know your life, and it sometimes gets facts wrong. You decide what to ask and what to use.
Words to know:
- AI: artificial intelligence: computer programs that do tasks like writing and answering questions.
- AI assistant: an AI program you chat with by typing or talking.
Try it now: Write down three tasks from your own week where an AI assistant could help you, your family or your community group.
You can now say what an AI assistant is and name three ways it could help you.

options: A person who reads your mail
A program you write or talk to in your own words
check.why: An AI assistant is a program that writes back an answer when you ask in your own words.

check.q: Your child is stuck on homework. How could an AI assistant help?
options: Do the whole test for them
Explain the topic in simpler words
check.why: AI can explain things in simpler words; you and your child stay in charge.

lessons.title: Lesson 3: Opening a free AI assistant and asking your first question
lessons.text:
Lesson 3 of 6 · about 5 minutes
Goal: Open a free AI assistant and ask it a clear question about a real task.
This lesson builds toward: Using a library computer or a phone, you will open a free AI assistant from its official app or website and ask a question with what you need, your situation and how you want the answer, without help.
On a library or community-center computer, open the web browser and go to copilot.microsoft.com, chatgpt.com or gemini.google.com. On a phone, install the official app from the app store.
Look for the box where you type. Ask your question the way you would ask a helpful neighbor: say what you need, a little about your situation, and how you want the answer.
For example: "I have $60 for groceries this week for a family of four. Give me five cheap dinner ideas with a shopping list. Use simple words."
Step by step:
- Open the browser or the official app.
- Find the message box.
- Type what you need, your situation (no private details), and how you want the answer.
- Press Enter or tap the send arrow, then read the answer.
Words to know:
- Browser: the program you use to visit websites, like Chrome, Edge or Safari.
- Prompt: the question or request you type to an AI assistant.
Try it now: Open a free AI assistant. Ask it for help with one task from your list in Lesson 2, using all three parts of a good question. Read the answer.
You can now open a free AI assistant and ask a clear question that gets a useful answer.

check.q: On a library computer, where do you type copilot.microsoft.com?
options: In the web browser's address bar
In an email to the library
check.why: You open the web browser and type the address to reach the AI assistant.

check.q: You want help planning a birthday party on a small budget. Which question is best?
options: "Help me plan a party for 8 kids with $50. Give me a simple list."
check.why: It says what you need, your situation and how you want the answer.

chapters.name: Chapter 2: Using AI for real life, safely

lessons.title: Lesson 4: Turning a hard letter into plain words
lessons.text:
Lesson 4 of 6 · about 5 minutes
Goal: Use an AI assistant to explain a confusing letter and make a to-do list.
This lesson builds toward: Given a confusing letter or notice, you will ask an AI assistant to explain it in plain words and make a to-do list with dates, using placeholders for private details, with no real names or numbers in the prompt.
Letters from schools, clinics, landlords and agencies can be full of hard words. An AI assistant can put them into plain words and pull out what you need to do and by when.
First, take out private details. Type or paste only the words that explain what the letter is about, and replace names and numbers with placeholders like [my name] or [account number].
Then ask: "Explain this letter in plain words. What do I need to do, and by what date? Make a short to-do list."
Step by step:
- Read the letter once and circle the parts you do not understand.
- Copy or type those parts, replacing names and numbers with placeholders.
- Ask the AI to explain it in plain words and make a to-do list with dates.
- Ask a follow-up if anything is still unclear, like "What does 'recertification' mean?"
Words to know:
- Placeholder: a stand-in like [my name] that you type instead of real private details.
- Follow-up: a second question that builds on the first answer.
Try it now: Choose a letter or notice you have (or a sample from a school website). Remove private details, then ask an AI assistant to explain it and make a to-do list.
You can now turn a confusing letter into plain words and a to-do list, with your private details left out.

check.q: Which is a good placeholder in a prompt?
check.why: A placeholder like [account number] stands in for the real detail so it stays private.

check.q: The AI's explanation still uses the word "recertification" and you do not know it. What do you do?
check.why: A follow-up question asks the AI to explain the hard word.

lessons.title: Lesson 5: Checking what AI tells you
lessons.text:
Lesson 5 of 6 · about 4 minutes
Goal: Check a date, phone number or rule from an AI answer with the official source.
This lesson builds toward: Given an AI answer with a date, phone number or rule, you will check it against the letter, the official .gov website, the office or 211, before you act on it.
AI assistants can be wrong. They might give an old phone number, the wrong deadline, or a rule from a different state.
Before you act on anything about money, benefits, health, school, housing or the law, check it. Look at the letter itself, the official website (government sites in the United States usually end in .gov), or call the office.
If you cannot find the answer, call 211. It is a free, confidential line that connects you to local help with food, housing, utilities and more.
Step by step:
- Circle every date, number and rule in the AI answer.
- Compare each one with the original letter.
- Check the official website or call the office.
- If you are stuck, call 211 or ask a librarian.
Words to know:
- .gov: the ending of official United States government website addresses.
- 211: a free, confidential phone line that connects people to local help.
Official sources:
- 211.org: About 211
Try it now: Take the to-do list from Lesson 4. Check one date or phone number against the original letter or the official website.
You can now check an AI answer against the official source before you act on it.

options: A free, confidential line that connects you to local help
check.why: 211 is free and confidential and connects people to local help like food and utilities.

check.q: The AI gives a phone number for the housing office. What do you do before calling?
options: Check it on the office's official website or on your letter
Ask the AI if it is sure
check.why: AI can give old or wrong numbers, so you check the official source first.

lessons.title: Lesson 6: Protecting your information and your family
lessons.text:
Lesson 6 of 6 · about 5 minutes
Goal: Keep private information out of AI tools and spot a scam message.
This lesson builds toward: When you write a prompt or get an urgent message, you will keep private information out and spot the warning signs of a scam, sharing no private numbers and contacting agencies only through a number or site you found yourself.
Never type these into an AI assistant: Social Security numbers, case or benefit numbers, bank or card numbers, passwords, or your children's full names with their school.
Scammers target families who are struggling. Watch out for messages that promise free money or government grants, say your benefits will stop unless you act right now, or ask you to pay with gift cards.
Real agencies do not ask for payment in gift cards. If a message worries you, do not click its links. Go to the official website yourself or call a number you already know.
Step by step:
- Read every prompt before you send it and remove private details.
- Be suspicious of messages that rush you or promise free money.
- Never pay with gift cards because a message told you to.
- Contact the agency using a number or website you found yourself.
Words to know:
- Scam: a trick to steal money or information.
- Phishing: a fake message that tries to get you to click a link or share private details.
Try it now: Final task: take a real letter or notice, remove all private details, ask an AI assistant to explain it and make a to-do list with dates, then check one date or phone number with the official source.
You can now use AI for a real family task while keeping your information safe and spotting scams.
How your final task is checked:
What we look at Not yet Meets Exceeds Private details removed The prompt has a real name, case number, account number or address. Every private name and number is left out or replaced with a placeholder. Uses clear placeholders like [my name] so the answer still makes sense. Clear request The request is vague, like "help with this". Says what you need, your situation and how you want the answer. The first answer is close to what you need. Plain words and to-do list No plain-words explanation or no to-do list. Gets a plain-words explanation and a short to-do list with dates. Asked a follow-up to explain a hard word or a step. Fact checked No date or phone number was checked. Checked one date or phone number against the letter or official source. Can say where they checked it and what they found. To pass: Meets or Exceeds on every row. If a row is Not yet, fix that part and try again.

check.q: Which is a warning sign of a scam?
options: A letter that matches the agency's website
A reminder from your child's school office
A message that rushes you to pay with gift cards
A bill with the right amount
check.why: Real agencies do not ask for gift cards or rush you to pay right now.

check.q: A text says you won a government grant and has a link. What do you do?
options: Click the link to claim it
Do not click; look up the agency yourself
check.why: Going to the official site or a number you found yourself keeps you safe from fake links.
